A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the landscape model is a valuable tool to assess contaminant fate, transport and exposure in a landscape context, and that landscape re-emission of Hg is an important source of Hg deposition in remote locations.
Hg deposition is not always well correlated with distance from point sources, and that Hg deposition can be highly variable even in regions remote from major point sources.
Hg deposition is a complex function of distance, prevailing wind, and landscape features.
The main takeaway from our work is that
landscape-scale Hg deposition can be quantified using sediment core data and the resulting spatial-temporal maps of deposition can be used as a guide to identify and prioritize areas for remediation.

sediment cores can be used to construct quantitative, high-resolution records of atmospheric deposition of contaminants, and that these data can be applied to reconstruct contaminant deposition on the landscape.
